extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing news stories of interviews, speeches, court proceedings, fires, accidents, and weather — covering leads, body construction, accuracy, and feature selection for newspaper reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads for speeches (feature choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter may begin a speech story by featuring: (i) the speaker's theme; (2) the title of the address; (3) a sentence or paragraph of forceful direct quotation; (4) an indirect quotation of dynamic statements; (5) the speaker's name; (6) the occasion of the speech; or (7) the time or the place of delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any one of these may be played up according to its importance in the address; choose the feature that best conveys the import of the speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featuring a single sentence (quotation lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quotation of a single sentence or a single paragraph is happiest if one can be found that will give the keynote of the speech or will harmonize with a declared policy of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when a sentence encapsulates the speech's keynote; examples provided. Ensure the quotation truly reflects the speech as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random statements as feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Play up in the lead even a random statement if it happens to agree with a specific policy or campaign to which the paper has committed itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a statement is valuable because it appears unprejudiced; conversely, ignore random statements opposed to the paper's views. Always make clear the precise relation of the featured quotation to the speech as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect quotation lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote indirectly in the lead a single statement of a speaker to shift an important point to the very first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indirect quotation when you need to present an important point immediately without implying verbatim quoting; e.g., 'that an inordinate indulgence... was the statement of Allen A. Pendel...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Title-featured lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the subject or title of the speech as the feature when it is particularly felicitous or expresses the theme of the address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advisable when the title itself is striking or summarises the address; examples show simple title leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme-featured lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature the theme when a single-sentence quotation cannot readily be found and the subject does not indicate the nature of the address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the theme succinctly in the lead; avoid overlong summarizing leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary lead (avoid long ones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Long summarizing leads of speeches are to be avoided as a rule because they are liable to become overloaded and cumbersome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a summarizing lead, keep individual clauses short and simple and make clear relations among clauses. Prefer short development followed by quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker's name as lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the speaker's name first only when he is sufficiently prominent locally or nationally to justify featuring him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature a famous or notable speaker by name; otherwise, choose another feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featuring the occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature the occasion or the auspices of the speech only when the speech and the speaker are of minor importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when occasion itself is the main newsworthy element (e.g., first congress of a kind); otherwise avoid making occasion primary if speech or speaker matters more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featuring time and place
rubrics_metrics.description: Rarely feature the time or the place, except when either is sufficiently important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use time/place leads only when they add notable interest (e.g., speaking from a barn door in pouring rain to a specific audience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Featuring several details (long summarizing lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: When speaker, subject, occasion, and place are all important it may be necessary to make a long summarizing lead of several paragraphs explaining these features in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to use a quarter- or half-column to explain multiple important elements before getting to the address itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence with the lead (body construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of the story should strive for proper coherence with the lead; avoid the incongruity of a clever epigrammatic lead followed by unrelated quoted statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continue a quotation lead with one or two development paragraphs, then follow with relevant quotations; do not slavishly follow the speaker's exact order if it damages coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and fairness in speech reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Only what one has taken down verbatim should be put within quotation marks; all else should be reported indirectly with determination to convey the real spirit of the lecture or sermon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not put non-verbatim passages in quotes; misunderstandings can lead to denials. Avoid playing up isolated subtopics that misrepresent the speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech story as a whole (presentation and signals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story as a whole should be a little speech in itself; the writer must mark clearly when statements are condensations and when they are direct quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use connecting phrases ('said he', 'continued the speaker') in unemphatic positions and vary their form; intersperse descriptive phrases about gestures, facial expressions, and manner to enliven the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series of speeches (prioritization)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting a series of speeches, play up at length the strongest address or the speech of the most important personage, then summarize remaining talks in a paragraph or so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all are equal, lead with general trend or a startling collective statement; when quoting multiple speakers, begin each quoted paragraph with the speaker's name for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banquets, conventions, and social occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: If speeches are unimportant or not delivered, feature the occasion, unusual incidents, persons attending, novelty of favors, originality of the menu, or the purpose and expected results of a convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for human-interest features (styles, parades, athletic contests) or untoward accidents that may supplant routine elements as the story's focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting current magazine articles and publications
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories of articles in current magazines, books, government publications, etc., are like addresses: lead may feature theme, title, author, a sentence, the publishing society, or motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extended analysis or scholarly catalogues of errors; report only those details of interest to the paper's readers rather than instructing the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court lead varies with stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead for court stories varies greatly according to the stage of proceedings: verdict leads feature guilt/innocence, penalty, or rehearing applications; intermediate-stage leads may feature cause, significant testimony, important witness, point reached, probable length, or clashes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the most newsworthy element for the lead depending on whether the trial concluded or continued; tailor the lead to the immediate development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court story body (quoting and legal language)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting trials, generally a more readable story is had by reporting testimony continuously and omitting the questions; avoid quoting long extracts of decisions owing to heavy legal expression unless form and language are vital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasionally quote verbatim questions and answers when depositions require it; when trials continue, connect the story to what has gone before so readers who missed prior coverage can understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous court stories — caution on libel and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid writing court stories humorously at the expense of accuracy and the feelings of those involved; libel can arise from wrong street numbers, misspelled names, misplaced words, and accidental resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the truth; do not warp facts to make a good story; be aware of the potential harm to innocent people and to the paper's credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead elements for fire stories (who, what, when, where, why, how, how much)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily the lead to a fire story should tell what was destroyed, the location of the property, the extent of the damage, the occupants or owners, the time, the cause, and what made the loss possible — answering who, what, when, where, why, how, and how much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include as many of these elements as are material; for example: what destroyed, owner, loss amount, insurance status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority: lives lost or endangered
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of, or danger to, life should take precedence over every other particular in a fire lead unless other features are exceptional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature casualty counts prominently and lead with deaths or serious injuries when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lists of killed or wounded (formatting rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a number of persons have been killed or injured, separate the names of the dead from those of the injured (dead first); record names in alphabetical order (surnames first); put each name with age, address, occupation, nature and extent of injury, and care given in a separate paragraph; underscore names for display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this structured list format so printing and reader lookup are straightforward; example layout provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts of heroism as features
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of heroism involving danger to or loss of life are always good features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead or strongly feature self-sacrifice or heroic deeds; these are reliable human-interest elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remarkable escapes as features
rubrics_metrics.description: Remarkable escapes from burning buildings or accidents make valuable features because of their elemental appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize dramatic means of escape and vivid details; these hold reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous, pathetic, or daring incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous, pathetic, or daring incidents are worth featuring strongly, particularly when they involve children, aged persons, or animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such incidents can humanize the story; use them with care and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of fire (feature when unusual or mysterious)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of the fire, if unusual or mysterious, may be featured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play up unusual causes (e.g., costume/prop causing blaze) but investigate before asserting cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buildings or property as features
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature particular buildings if especially valuable by reason of their age, location, or cost of construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic or economically important properties warrant prominent attention and estimated loss figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other fire features to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Other particulars that may be featured include occupants, owners, prominent persons involved, amount and character of the damage, amount of insurance, how the fire was discovered, how it spread, when the alarm was given, and the promptness or delay of the fire department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select any of these particulars provided it has unusual importance or interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of the fire story (damage, insurance, eyewitnesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The body of the fire story should include the extent of the damage and the amount of insurance; quote direct statements of eyewitnesses or injured persons to add interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use janitor's accounts, personal anecdotes, and eyewitness quotes to add action and human detail; include verified insurance and loss figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rumors at fires — verify or omit
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard against wild rumors about extent of loss, numbers injured or burned, certainty of arson, etc.; never take such stories at face value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate until details are accurate; if they cannot be proved, omit them or record them explicitly as rumors. Maintain composure amid pandemonium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accident stories general plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Accident stories generally follow the same constructive plans as fires: the lead should play up number of lives lost or endangered, cause of the accident, extent of damage or injury, time, and place — answering who, what, when, where, why, and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature any one of these elements according to importance; when many killed or hurt, use the prescribed lists; body may continue in simple chronological order, reserving important details till later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather stories: types and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Weather stories belong with accidents when they cause harm; a severe atmospheric disturbance is told as a simple narrative of events, while routine daily forecasts require felicity of language to remain interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For damaging storms, report casualties, damage, and disruption plainly. For routine forecasts, strive for original, readable language to avoid monotony.
